documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: When a deal ended or changed, the company sued the state
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services, or held mining rights, have used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts, took services back or stopped a deal, including when protests forced it. Most of these claims went to ICSID, the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in Washington, which its own website calls "one of the five organizations of the World Bank Group". The legal basis was usually a bilateral investment treaty, an agreement between two countries that lets a company from one sue the other.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Aid money that goes back to companies in the donor country
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
Tied aid is aid that must be spent on goods or services from the country that gave it. Eurodad, a European network of groups working on debt and aid, counted about $26.9 billion of tied aid in 2018, or 21% of bilateral and EU aid. Its total for formal and informal tying together is at least $32.3 billion and possibly up to $37.9 billion. It puts the direct short-term cost of tying at $2 billion to $7 billion.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: Two studies measure aid against UN politics. documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Funds that buy old debt and sue in New York and London
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
When a country cannot pay, most lenders usually accept a reduced deal. A holdout refuses and sues for the full amount. A vulture fund is the critics' name for a fund that buys defaulted debt to do this. An ECB working paper (no. 2135, 2018) by Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein counted 158 cases against 34 defaulting governments from 1976 to 2010: 130 in US courts (82.3%), 23 in the UK (14.6%) and 5 in arbitration. New York law governs almost half of outstanding sovereign bonds (White & Case, 2024) or over 50% (Insurance Journal, 2026).

documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: The Paris Club is an informal group of creditor governments, dating to 1956, that reschedules loans together, case by case and tied to an IMF-backed programme. Lex Rieffel, a former US Treasury desk officer for it, writes that "China, however, is not a member," and lists it among ad hoc participants. documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
Foreign direct investment earns income for its owners, and part stays in the host country. UNCTAD, the UN trade and development body, reports $1.5 trillion of this income in 2011 on $21 trillion of investment, a 7% return: 8% in developing economies, 13% in transition economies and 5% in developed countries. Globally in 2011, nearly one-third stayed in host economies and two-thirds went back to investors.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: UNCTAD said in 2015 that about 30% of cross-border corporate investment passes through offshore hubs, and estimated developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to those hubs. Across developing economies, each 10 percentage points of offshore investment goes with a 1-point lower rate of return. IMF economists Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen wrote in 2019 that phantom investment, money passing through empty companies, comes to $15 trillion, almost 40% of global FDI, up from about 30% less than a decade earlier. documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: A government can give a UN body or other multilateral organisation "core" money, which the organisation decides how to spend, or "earmarked" money, which the donor ties to a country, topic or project. hyps.title: Aid programmes used as cover for spies
hyps.conviction: Four cases are on the public record, each exposed by accident. Whether the practice continues is the suspicion.
story: In 2011 a Pakistani doctor named Shakil Afridi went door to door in the town of Abbottabad offering hepatitis B vaccinations. The drive was run for the CIA, which was trying to find out who was living in the walled compound where Osama bin Laden was hiding. Afterwards the deans of US public health schools wrote that seven or more United Nations workers vaccinating Pakistani children against polio had been shot dead, and in May 2014 the White House promised that the CIA would make no operational use of vaccination programmes, a promise that covers vaccination and nothing else. The suspicion this entry describes is that Abbottabad was not a one-off: that rich governments have used their aid programmes, over and over, as cover for intelligence work and political operations inside other countries. If so, people who accept a vaccine, a police-training course or a new building from a foreign aid agency cannot know who is really behind it, and the danger falls on genuine aid workers.

The record goes back decades. From 1962 to 1974 the US aid agency, USAID, ran an Office of Public Safety that trained and equipped police abroad. Its director from 1962 to 1973, Byron Engle, is described in published histories as a CIA operative. By one historical count it sent about 1,500 advisers to at least 52 countries, and Congress ended it in 1974 after Senator James Abourezk set out to expose its activities amid accusations that it taught torture. Forty years later, in 2014, the Associated Press revealed that USAID had built ZunZuneo, a text-message network for Cubans, through front companies in Spain and the Cayman Islands, paid through foreign banks. By USAID's own count it had about 68,000 users before it shut down in September 2012, and they were not told who had made it. USAID said the programme was not covert.

Other governments have done the same. In 2004 Australia's foreign intelligence service, ASIS, placed listening devices in the walls of Timor-Leste's cabinet offices in Dili while they were being renovated under an Australian aid project, during negotiations over oil and gas in the Timor Sea. That case is told in full in the entry on spying at the negotiating table. Each of these came out by accident: congressional pressure in one, more than 1,000 pages of documents obtained by reporters in another, a retired spy's complaint in the third. The 1974 law that banned US training of foreign police had gained 'a dozen exemptions' by 1992, according to Senator Alan Cranston, whose remarks the Federation of American Scientists reproduces with a GAO report. No law in the United States or Australia requires the government to say whether intelligence officers work under aid cover today.

The question would be settled by the CIA's own records of how it used aid cover after 1974, the files the USAID inspector general opened on ZunZuneo in 2014, the records on ZunZuneo that the Senate Foreign Relations Committee demanded from USAID that year, and Australia's records of the aid project in Dili. If those show that the known cases were the whole of it, the suspicion fails.
hyps.missing: No count exists of intelligence use of aid cover after 1974. The USAID inspector general's 2014 file and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee records have not been located in published form.
hyps.would_settle: Declassified CIA records on use of aid cover after 1974; the USAID inspector general's 2014 ZunZuneo review; the records the Senate Foreign Relations Committee requested from USAID on ZunZuneo in 2014.

hyps.title: Aid money turns up in Swiss bank accounts
hyps.conviction: One peer-reviewed study, partly by a World Bank economist, measures the leak. Who moved the money, and why the Bank held the paper, are the suspicion.
story: In February 2020 a professor in Copenhagen, Niels Johannesen, posted a research paper on his own website. He had written it with Jørgen Juel Andersen and the World Bank's own economist Bob Rijkers, comparing World Bank aid payments to the 22 most aid-dependent countries with bank deposits recorded by the Bank for International Settlements. In the quarters when a country received aid worth 1 per cent of its national income, its deposits in offshore centres known for bank secrecy rose by 3.4 per cent, while its deposits in ordinary financial centres did not move, so that about 7.5 per cent of the aid appeared to leak out, with the rise driven by accounts in Switzerland and Luxembourg. The Economist reported that the paper had passed the Bank's internal review in November 2019 but that higher officials blocked publication, and linked the resignation of the Bank's chief economist, Pinelopi Goldberg, after less than 15 months, to the paper. Within hours of Johannesen posting it, the Bank published it; it later passed peer review in the Journal of Political Economy. The suspicion is that a steady slice of the money lent and given to the poorest countries ends up in the private accounts of the people who run them, and that the lenders would rather not count it.

An older line of research found the same thing in loans. The economists Léonce Ndikumana and James Boyce estimated capital flight from 33 sub-Saharan African countries between 1970 and 2004 at $443 billion in 2004 dollars, against foreign debts of $195 billion, which makes the region a net creditor to the rest of the world. In their analysis, roughly 60 cents of every dollar borrowed abroad left again as capital flight in the same year. In their book Africa's Odious Debts they write that a significant part ended up in private accounts at the same banks that had made the loans. On this map, the documented pattern on investment routed through tax havens shows how companies use the same havens.

Neither study can say whose money it was. Both rest on country totals, Swiss and other haven banks do not publish who holds their accounts, and no public record traces where a disbursement went after it reached a government's account. That is why the evidence is statistical rather than a list of names.

What would settle it is account-level information: records from the haven banks of deposits from officials in the weeks after aid or loans were paid out, which tax authorities can now obtain under information-exchange treaties. Two further records would help: the Bank's internal correspondence on why the 2020 paper was held, and the same test run on IMF lending, regional development banks and individual donor governments.
hyps.missing: The same method has not been applied to IMF, regional bank or bilateral donor disbursements. No account-level records are public.
hyps.would_settle: Account-level haven deposit records matched to disbursement dates; the World Bank's internal correspondence on the paper's review; the method rerun on other lenders.

countries.note: By far the most important haven among those with country-level data; with Luxembourg, drove the rise.

hyps.title: Global rankings bent for countries with money to give
hyps.conviction: A law firm's investigation found the rankings were changed for China and Saudi Arabia. Whether this was routine is the suspicion.
story: In 2017 Kristalina Georgieva, then chief executive of the World Bank, went to the home of a manager on the Bank's Doing Business team to collect a printed copy of the final report, and thanked the employee for helping to resolve the problem. That is one detail from an investigation by the law firm WilmerHale, published in September 2021, which found that staff had changed China's data under pressure from the office of the Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, and from Georgieva, at a time when the Bank was seeking China's support for a large increase in its capital. The changes put China at 78th in the 2018 edition, seven places higher than the draft data had it. Georgieva said she disagreed fundamentally with the findings, and the IMF's board, where she had become managing director, backed her in October 2021. Doing Business ranked 190 countries on how easy they made it to start and run a company; investors used it and governments rewrote laws to climb it. The suspicion is that global rankings like this are bent for countries the institution needs or that pay it, and that the scoring itself pushed countries to strip protections from workers.

China was not the only case. For the 2020 edition, WilmerHale found that senior staff changed Saudi Arabia's data. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named the top improver, and it had paid the Bank for advisory work aimed at improving the very indicators being scored. In 2006 Saudi Arabia's king had said he wanted the country among the top ten by 2010. WilmerHale found no evidence that the president's office or the board were involved in the 2020 changes. The Bank cancelled Doing Business.

There had been warnings. In January 2018 the Bank's chief economist, Paul Romer, said Chile had fallen in the rankings because of changes in method rather than in Chile, and suggested politics might be behind it. He then said he had not meant to suggest manipulation, and resigned; Augusto Lopez-Claros, who had directed the group that published the rankings, called the claim that the changes targeted Chile wholly without merit. The rankings also shaped laws. Until 2009 they scored countries higher for weaker worker protections, through what was called the employing workers indicator. The Bank suspended that indicator in 2009 after pressure from unions, the International Labour Organization and the US Congress, and an independent panel the Bank set up in 2013 recommended removing it permanently.

WilmerHale examined two editions. What would settle whether China and Saudi Arabia were exceptions is the full record of original and final data for every country in every edition from 2003, with each change and who asked for it. The Bank's new Business Ready ranking, launched in 2024, brings a labour topic back, so the same record matters again.
hyps.missing: The full data change log across all Doing Business editions has not been published.
hyps.would_settle: Original and final data for every country in every Doing Business edition, 2003 to 2020, with each change and its requester.

hyps.title: Chinese-financed ports that may be future naval bases
hyps.conviction: One base opened after years of denial, a second facility hosting Chinese warships, and a researched shortlist of eight more. That port lending is laying the ground for bases is the suspicion.
story: For years China said it had no plans for a military base in Djibouti, on the Horn of Africa. It confirmed one in November 2015 and opened it in 2017. The suspicion is that some of the ports China has paid for or built around the world were planned with a second purpose: places where its navy could dock, refuel and one day be based, with the loans giving Beijing the leverage to ask. If so, a country taking a Chinese loan for a harbour may also be signing up, without saying so, to a side in a future conflict.

Cambodia's Ream naval base is the case being watched. In 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported an agreement giving China's navy use of the base for 30 years; both governments denied it. China paid to rebuild Ream, and satellite images showed a new pier almost identical to the one at Djibouti and long enough to berth Chinese aircraft carriers. Two Chinese warships berthed there from December 2023. Cambodia formally opened the rebuilt Ream in April 2025 and declared it open to foreign navies, and a US warship visited in early 2026. In 2023 AidData counted 123 Chinese-financed seaport projects at 78 ports in 46 countries, worth $29.9 billion, and named the eight most likely places for China's next bases: Hambantota in Sri Lanka, Bata in Equatorial Guinea, Gwadar in Pakistan, Kribi in Cameroon, Ream, Luganville in Vanuatu, Nacala in Mozambique and Nouakchott in Mauritania. It also noted that none of them is currently militarily defensible.

One famous version of this story does not hold. Hambantota is often described as a port China seized when Sri Lanka could not pay. Research for Chatham House found otherwise: the 2017 99-year lease to China Merchants Port was a new investment of $1.12 billion, not a swap of debt for the port, the Chinese loans for the port were only 4.8 per cent of the government's foreign debt, and Sri Lanka got no debt relief from it. So the suspicion is not a debt trap. It is that commercial ports are being chosen and built so they can serve a navy too. On this map, Hambantota's industrial zone met protests over the taking of village and farm land, and Gwadar's port and new expressway have pushed fishers off their homes and fishing routes.

The port contracts and loan agreements are mostly unpublished, which is where any clause giving warships access would sit. What would settle the question is publication of those contracts, and the records of which naval vessels call at the eight shortlisted ports over the coming years. Repeated long stays by Chinese warships would confirm the suspicion; their absence would weaken it.
hyps.missing: Port concession and loan contracts for the eight shortlisted ports are unpublished; no consolidated log of naval port calls.
hyps.would_settle: Publication of the concession and loan contracts for the shortlisted ports; naval port-call records for those ports over time.

hyps.title: Carbon credits driving a new land grab
hyps.conviction: Agreements covering a fifth of Zimbabwe and a tenth of Liberia and Zambia, a court ruling against Kenya's largest soil-carbon project, and evictions rights groups have linked to carbon deals. That carbon finance is driving evictions is the suspicion.
story: On 2 November 2023, the Kenyan government began evicting the Ogiek, an Indigenous people who have lived in the Mau Forest for generations, from their homes at Sasimwani. Survival International counted about 167 houses destroyed, including a school. A few weeks earlier Kenya had signed an agreement with a Dubai company, Blue Carbon, to produce carbon credits on millions of hectares. Amnesty International, Minority Rights Group and Survival International put out a joint statement asking whether carbon credits were behind the evictions. The government said it was protecting the environment, and Blue Carbon told the BBC it had no ongoing projects in Kenya. The suspicion is that the market in carbon credits, which lets companies pay for forests to be protected so they can count that against their own emissions, is driving a new land grab in poor countries, in which governments sign huge areas over to foreign firms and the people living there are fenced out.

Blue Carbon was set up in 2022 and is chaired by a member of Dubai's ruling family, Sheikh Ahmed Dalmook Al Maktoum. During 2023 it signed agreements covering about a fifth of Zimbabwe (7.5 million hectares), about a tenth of Zambia (8 million hectares), 8 million hectares of Tanzania's forest reserves and about a tenth of Liberia (around 1 million hectares), altogether an area about the size of the United Kingdom. Under the leaked Liberian agreement, the company would take 70 per cent of the income for the first ten years. Liberia's government later said its deal had been stopped, and an AFP investigation in 2025 found that other deals had also gone nowhere.

Where carbon projects have gone ahead, a court and the main certifier have found problems. In northern Kenya, the Northern Rangelands Trust runs a soil-carbon project covering more than 2 million hectares across 14 community conservancies, selling credits to companies including Netflix and Meta. In January 2025 a Kenyan court ruled that two of its largest conservancies had been set up unconstitutionally, with no basis in law; one of them produced about a fifth of the project's credits. Verra, the main body that certifies carbon credits, suspended the project in 2023 and again in 2025, and reinstated it in 2026. This map holds earlier cases of the same kind: the Sengwer evicted from Embobut Forest in 2014, and carbon projects in Peru, Cambodia, Kenya and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Most carbon agreements between governments and companies are not published, and Liberia's became known only because it leaked. What would settle the question is the full set of carbon-rights agreements signed since 2020, together with the registries of certified projects, checked against court records and documented evictions in the same areas. A count of how many registered land-based carbon projects overlap with evictions would show whether the cases here are exceptions or the pattern.
hyps.missing: No count of registered land-based carbon projects overlapping documented evictions.
hyps.would_settle: All government carbon-rights agreements since 2020 and carbon registry project boundaries, checked against court records and documented evictions.

hyps.title: Bribes built into the contracts that loans pay for
hyps.conviction: Court convictions in Lesotho and a record settlement by Siemens show bribery on lender-financed contracts. That bribes are a routine cost built into such contracts, and passed on to borrowers, is the suspicion.
story: Between 1988 and 1998 Masupha Sole, the chief executive of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a set of dams sending water from the mountains of Lesotho to Johannesburg, took about $2 million in bribes paid through middlemen on behalf of 12 international construction and engineering firms. Some of the money went into his Swiss bank accounts. The World Bank lent to the project. Lesotho, one of the world's poorest countries, prosecuted: Sole was sentenced to 18 years, reduced to 15 on appeal, and the Canadian firm Acres International and the German firm Lahmeyer International were convicted. The World Bank barred Acres from its contracts for three years in 2004 and Lahmeyer for seven in 2006, and critics said the Bank had moved slowly. The suspicion is that bribery is a routine cost of winning contracts paid for by development loans, built into the price, and that the borrowing country repays the loan, bribe included.

Siemens, the German engineering company, showed how routine it could be. In December 2008 it agreed to pay about $1.6 billion in fines and penalties in the United States and Germany. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said it had made 4,283 separate payments totalling about $1.4 billion to bribe officials around the world between 2001 and 2007. A US official described bribery at the company as standard operating procedure. In a separate settlement with the World Bank, Siemens agreed to spend $100 million over 15 years on anti-corruption work and to stay out of Bank business for two years, after a Russian subsidiary was found to have engaged in corrupt practices on a Bank-financed transport project in Moscow.

Companies are caught when a borrowing government is willing to prosecute, when a rich country's regulator acts, as the United States did with Siemens, or when the World Bank's own investigators find the evidence, as they did with Siemens's Russian subsidiary. The World Bank's debarment list records only the firms that were caught.

What would settle how common this is are the full investigation files behind the World Bank's debarments, and a comparison of prices on lender-financed contracts with the prices the same firms charged for similar work elsewhere. A consistent premium on financed contracts would show the cost being passed on to borrowers.
hyps.missing: No price comparison between lender-financed contracts and comparable unfinanced work by the same firms.
hyps.would_settle: World Bank debarment investigation files; a price comparison of lender-financed contracts against comparable work by the same firms.

hyps.title: Seed laws pushed on poor countries that restrict farmers' own seed
hyps.conviction: The World Bank's own agriculture rankings scored seed laws, and its loans have required seed certification laws as conditions. That this serves seed companies at farmers' expense is the suspicion.
story: In 2016 the World Bank held up Tanzania as a model for having joined the 1991 version of the UPOV Convention, an international treaty that protects the rights of those who breed new plant varieties. Under Tanzania's seed laws, farmers who save, swap or sell protected seed, as their families have done for generations, can face fines or prison. The praise came in a new World Bank ranking, Enabling the Business of Agriculture, which the Bank launched in 2013 at the request of the G8 group of rich countries to score how well each country's laws suited agribusiness. The suspicion is that the lenders are using rankings and loan conditions to rewrite seed laws across Africa and Asia for the benefit of a handful of large seed and chemical companies, and against the farmers who supply most of their own seed.

The rankings were backed by loan conditions. The aid agency CAFOD went through 15 years of World Bank documents and found two requirements that countries had to meet before receiving agricultural loans: subsidies tied to buying hybrid seed and the fertiliser that goes with it, in Mali, Niger, Kenya and Guinea between 2017 and 2020, and seed certification laws that limit what small farmers can grow, save, share and sell, in the Central African Republic, Chad, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Mozambique and Nigeria. CAFOD notes that across Africa farmers' own seed systems supply about 80 per cent of the seed they plant. In 2017, 157 organisations and academics signed a statement against the ranking's seed scoring, and the Oakland Institute reported that it had already inspired a new seed ordinance in Rwanda opening the way to UPOV.

The Bank says its seed indicators measure laws and rules that support the timely release of new seed to farmers and acknowledges that farmers also use informal seed. But a ranking that scores only the formal seed market, and a loan that requires certification laws, push in one direction, and six Western firms control over two-thirds of the world's commercial seed sales, according to the Oakland Institute. Who asked for each seed condition, and who drafted the laws that followed, is not part of the published loan documents.

What would settle it is the drafting history of the seed laws passed after these loans and rankings, including which consultants and companies were involved, and a count of how far the share of certified seed bought from foreign companies rose in the countries that changed their laws.
hyps.missing: No drafting history of post-loan seed laws; no count of foreign seed-company market share before and after.
hyps.would_settle: Drafting records of seed laws passed after World Bank conditions or rankings; certified-seed market shares by supplier before and after.

hyps.title: Hedge funds that buy poor countries' debt cheap and sue for the full price
hyps.conviction: Court records show funds buying defaulted debt of poor or bankrupt countries at a fraction of its value and winning many times what they paid. That this is a business built on blocking debt relief, protected by the courts of rich countries, is the suspicion.
story: On 2 October 2012 a court in Ghana ordered the ARA Libertad, a three-masted training ship of the Argentine navy, held at the port of Tema, with more than 300 people on board, until Argentina paid a hedge fund. The fund, NML Capital, belonged to the New York billionaire Paul Singer's Elliott Management and held Argentine bonds left unpaid since Argentina's default of 2001. Most of Argentina's creditors had accepted a reduced deal; NML had bought its bonds cheaply and held out for full payment. The ship was released in December, after the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ordered Ghana to let it go. NML's lawsuits in New York went on. In 2016 Argentina's new government paid four holdout funds $4.65 billion. NML received about $2.28 billion, about 369 per cent of the face value of its bonds, and the economists Martín Guzmán and Joseph Stiglitz estimated its return on what it had paid at about 1,180 per cent. The suspicion is that a group of investment funds has built a business on buying the debts of poor and bankrupt countries for a few cents, refusing the relief other creditors agree to, and suing in London and New York for the full amount, so that money freed by debt relief flows to them instead of to the people it was meant for.

Zambia, one of the poorest countries in the world, met the same kind of fund. In 1999 Donegal International, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, bought for about $3.2 million a debt Zambia owed to Romania for farm machinery, with a principal of $29.8 million. When Zambia fell behind on a settlement, Donegal sued in London in 2005 for more than $55 million. The judge found Donegal's witnesses at times evasive and dishonest but held Zambia to the settlement, and Zambia agreed in 2007 to pay about $15.5 million. Zambia was then receiving debt relief from rich governments and the World Bank.

These were not isolated cases. A United Nations independent expert reported in 2010 that, according to the World Bank and the IMF, 54 court cases had been brought by commercial creditors against 12 heavily indebted poor countries between 1998 and 2008. In June 2022, as Sri Lanka ran out of dollars for food and fuel, Hamilton Reserve Bank, a small bank in St Kitts and Nevis, sued it in New York for full payment on more than $250 million of bonds, more than a quarter of the issue and enough to block a restructuring of it. Britain passed a law in 2010 limiting what such funds can recover from the poorest countries in British courts, and Belgium followed in 2015. New York, where most sovereign bonds are governed, has no such law.

What the funds paid for the debt is almost never disclosed, which is why the size of their profits is mostly estimated. What would settle how large the business is would be a register of who buys the debt of countries in crisis, at what price, and how much they later collect through settlements and courts, set against the debt relief the same countries received from everyone else.
hyps.missing: No register of who buys distressed sovereign debt, at what price, and what they later recover.
hyps.would_settle: A register of purchases of distressed sovereign debt (buyer, price) matched with later court awards and settlements, set against relief given by other creditors.

hyps.title: Development money handed to private equity and for-profit hospitals
hyps.conviction: The collapse of Abraaj, backed by the Gates Foundation and development banks, led to US fraud charges and guilty pleas; Oxfam documented hospitals funded by development banks detaining patients who could not pay. That development lenders' turn to private equity routinely lets money meant for the poor be skimmed or spent on care the poor cannot reach is the suspicion.
story: In early 2018 four investors in a $1 billion health fund, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the World Bank's private-sector arm the International Finance Corporation, Britain's CDC Group and France's Proparco, hired forensic accountants to find out what had happened to about $200 million they had put in to build hospitals and clinics in poor countries such as Pakistan, India and Nigeria. The fund was run by the Abraaj Group, a Dubai private equity firm that managed almost $14 billion and whose founder, Arif Naqvi, had sat on a Davos panel with Bill Gates. Within months Abraaj collapsed in what Bloomberg called the world's biggest private-equity insolvency. In 2019 US prosecutors charged Naqvi and other executives with defrauding investors, and two former partners pleaded guilty. A British judge approved Naqvi's extradition in 2021, and in March 2023 the High Court refused his last challenge; he denies the charges. The suspicion is that, as aid agencies and development banks hand more of their money to private equity funds and for-profit companies, money meant for the poor is skimmed off in fees and fraud or spent on services the poor cannot afford, with little oversight.

Oxfam looked at where the money reached hospitals. In 2023 Oxfam traced more than 350 health investments made by the development finance arms of Britain, France, Germany, the European Union and the World Bank. It found that the Nairobi Women's Hospital in Kenya, funded by several of them, had held patients, including a newborn baby and a schoolboy, for months until their bills were paid, and had kept the body of one woman's mother for two years. In Lagos, the most basic maternity package at the funded Lagoon Hospitals cost more than nine years' income for the poorest tenth of Nigerians. Oxfam could not find a single disclosed evaluation that credibly measured what these investments did for low-income patients.

The investments often pass through layers of funds, and Oxfam reported that the development banks invest in the same health companies through the same intermediaries, many in tax havens, as this map's entry on development money flowing through tax havens describes. At an Indian chain backed by three of the lenders, CARE Hospitals, a family told Oxfam their injured child was refused treatment unless they paid $1,200; TPG, a shareholder in the chain, told Oxfam that patients are always treated in an emergency whatever their finances. The IFC told the Guardian that private providers can add to health systems' capacity.

What would settle it is disclosure, fund by fund, of how much development money went into private equity and for-profit health companies, what fees the fund managers took, and who the patients turned out to be, with independent audits of the funds' accounts. Abraaj's books were checked only after investors noticed money sitting unspent.
hyps.missing: No fund-by-fund disclosure of development money in private equity, the fees taken, or who was served.
hyps.would_settle: Fund-level disclosure of development-bank money placed with private equity and for-profit health firms, management fees, independent audits and patient income data.

hyps.title: Foreign companies that pay soldiers and militias to protect their profits
hyps.conviction: Chiquita and Lafarge pleaded guilty in US courts to paying groups designated as terrorists; company records showed Freeport paying Indonesian officers; Amnesty documented Shell's payments to Nigeria's security forces. That foreign companies routinely pay armed men who then kill local people is the suspicion.
story: In March 2007 Chiquita Brands, the American banana company, pleaded guilty in a US federal court to paying a Colombian paramilitary group, the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, known as the AUC. Through its Colombian subsidiary, Banadex, Chiquita had paid the AUC more than $1.7 million between 1997 and 2004 in the banana-growing regions of Urabá and Santa Marta, where the group was killing civilians, and the company kept paying more than $300,000 after the US Justice Department told it to stop. Chiquita paid a $25 million fine. Thousands of Colombians later sued over relatives killed by the group, and in June 2024 a federal jury in Florida found Chiquita liable for eight of those killings and ordered it to pay $38.3 million to their families. The suspicion is that foreign companies operating in poor and conflict-ridden countries routinely pay soldiers, police and militias to guard their mines, plantations and pipelines, knowing that the same men kill, beat and drive off the people who live nearby.

In December 2005 the New York Times reported, from company records, that the American mining company Freeport-McMoRan had given Indonesian military and police generals, colonels, majors, captains and units nearly $20 million between 1998 and 2004 around its Grasberg copper and gold mine in Papua, besides money for barracks and roads. Freeport said it had no alternative to relying on Indonesia's military and police, and that its payments were legal. In April 1995 the Australian Council for Overseas Aid had reported that at least 37 people, 22 of them civilians, were killed or disappeared around the mine in 1994 and early 1995, and that Freeport security staff joined the army in shootings, arrests and torture; Freeport and the Indonesian government denied the death figures.

In 2017 Amnesty International published a report drawing on thousands of pages of Shell's internal documents from Nigeria in the 1990s, when the Ogoni people were protesting against the company's oil pollution. Amnesty found that Shell had given the security forces logistical support and payments, which the head of Shell Nigeria from 1994 admitted was standard practice, and that it kept asking for military help after security forces had killed protesters and burned villages; Shell said it never colluded with the military or encouraged violence. In October 2022 the French cement company Lafarge pleaded guilty in the United States to paying the Islamic State and the al-Nusrah Front, through intermediaries, about $6 million in 2013 and 2014 to keep its $680 million plant in northern Syria running, and agreed to pay about $778 million. US officials said it was the first time a company had pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organisation.

These payments came out through prosecutions, a newspaper's access to company records and a human rights group's access to internal files. Companies are generally not required to publish what they pay to security forces abroad. What would settle how common this is would be mandatory, country-by-country disclosure of payments to soldiers, police and private armed groups by every company operating in conflict areas, matched against records of killings and evictions around their sites.
hyps.missing: No mandatory disclosure of company payments to security forces and armed groups abroad.
hyps.would_settle: Country-by-country disclosure of payments to soldiers, police and armed groups by companies in conflict areas, matched to records of killings and evictions near their sites.

hyps.title: Cities' water handed to foreign companies on the lenders' advice
hyps.conviction: World Bank lending and advice preceded water privatisations in Cochabamba, Jakarta and Manila, followed by sharp price rises, a fatal protest, and court and arbitration fights. That lenders pushed water privatisation for the benefit of a few multinationals is the suspicion.
story: In September 1999 the Bolivian government, in a process with a single bidder, gave the water system of Cochabamba, the country's third city, to Aguas del Tunari, a company controlled through offshore holdings by the American engineering company Bechtel, on a 40-year contract. According to the Democracy Center, a $14 million World Bank water loan had been conditioned on the city privatising its water. Within weeks bills rose by more than half on average, and in some homes by up to 200 per cent, in a country where the minimum wage was about $60 a month. Protests spread across the city, and in April 2000 the government declared a state of siege, soldiers shot dead a 17-year-old, Víctor Hugo Daza, and more than a hundred people were wounded, and the company left. Its owners moved its registration to the Netherlands to use a Dutch investment treaty and claimed at least $50 million from Bolivia at the World Bank's arbitration centre, having invested, by one estimate, less than $1 million; after an international campaign Bechtel and its Spanish partner Abengoa dropped the claim in January 2006 for a token two bolivianos, about 30 cents. The suspicion is that the World Bank and other lenders pushed poor countries to hand their cities' water to a handful of foreign companies, through loan conditions and advice, and that the companies profited while poor households paid more for water that did not improve.

Jakarta's water went the same way earlier. The World Bank lent Jakarta's water company $92 million in 1991 and assigned consultants who advised privatisation; a 1998 Bank report said the loan had facilitated it. In 1997, without open bidding, the city was split between Britain's Thames Water, whose local company gave 20 per cent to President Suharto's son, and France's Suez, partnered with the Salim Group of a Suharto associate. Tariffs rose by 35, 40 and 30 per cent in three years, and coverage reached only 59 per cent by 2015 against a 98 per cent target. In October 2017 Indonesia's Supreme Court found the privatisation had not improved water quality, quantity or continuity and ordered it ended.

In Manila, the World Bank's private-sector arm, the International Finance Corporation, drafted the 1997 concession agreement under a contract that paid it at least $1 million if the bidding succeeded, and later bought into one of the winning companies. Basic rates in the east zone rose 496 per cent between 1997 and 2003, and from late October 2003, 672 people in the poor Tondo district fell ill with gastroenteritis after the west zone operator, part-owned by Suez, allegedly lowered water pressure. Coverage did rise, from about 60 to over 80 per cent of people by 2002.

The published record shows lending, advice and, in Cochabamba, a reported loan condition, but not who drafted the advice or which companies were consulted beforehand. What would settle the question is the internal correspondence of the lenders on water privatisations in the 1990s and 2000s, set beside the list of companies that won the contracts and the advisory fees the lenders' own arms earned.
hyps.missing: Internal lender correspondence on water privatisations and the companies consulted is unpublished.
hyps.would_settle: Lender correspondence on 1990s-2000s water privatisations, set against the companies that won and the advisory fees earned by the lenders' own arms.
